paragraphs.subtitles_en: Plan B splits the army. Both groups rest at qualifying locations, then reunite. Here is an independent replay of B. During the checked rest window, both armies showed a current supply change of +20 per month. That was the current rate. It does not show that supply had already increased. Next, we observe actual soldier and supply changes separately. After the actual merge, we must check the regiments and commander again. There is still no observed London endpoint for B.

Plan C takes a different route, through verified waypoints to London. In this independent replay, on game day 77 after the shared start, we first observed the main army in London. It was still en route on day 75. It arrived between those observations. The exact moment is unknown. This main army started with 6,679 soldiers. At the arrival observation, it had 6,689: a net gain of ten. All 27 regiments retained their identities and maximum soldier counts. Supply fell from about 110.38 to 101.90. Supply capacity remained 300. Current attrition at the endpoint was 1%. That was the rate under current conditions. It does not tell us how many died en route. These figures describe the original main army. They are not the total soldiers in all player units.

In the earlier equal split, both armies inherited about 110.38 supply. The main army had capacity 300; the new group had capacity 100. Now look at this replay of B. Between days 20 and 21, the new group's supply fell from about 110.38 to 100. Both armies' soldier counts and full regiment readings were unchanged. The current monthly rate still showed +20. But the actual supply change was downward, back to capacity. This was neither reinforcement nor a supply increase from a low stock.

Next, consider two separate observation windows. Between days 26 and 27, the main army gained seven soldiers net; the new group gained three. Supply was unchanged at both endpoints. Between days 31 and 32, main-army supply rose from about 106.14 to 126.14. The new group had 100 at both endpoints. The full regiment roster and soldier counts were also unchanged. Record soldier changes and supply gains on their own dates. Do not edit them into a single update. Later, the two armies reunited at the same location and actually merged. Before merging, their supply was about 126.14 and 100. Apply each army's merge weight and round down each contribution. The result is about 113.06. After merging, capacity was 100, and actual supply was also 100. This window independently confirms the upper-cap clamp. A simple average of the two supply stocks cannot replace that calculation.

Align results by the same date or event. First check actual arrival, then the full regiments and available soldiers. Then check supply, reinforcement and attrition windows, and finally actual payments. After B's merge, all 27 original regiments remained. But a new regiment record appeared, with one soldier out of a maximum of one. The merged army had 6,690 soldiers, out of a maximum of 6,748. The commander also changed, breaking the conditions fixed at the start. The causes of the new record and commander change remain unconfirmed. So B stopped on day 38, with 52 days left in its budget. It stopped because the fixed conditions failed, not because time ran out. We can retain this as a sample of the merge mechanism. But it has no comparable London endpoint. C also had multiple sampling deviations. Pulses planned for at most one day actually advanced two. The later results are retained as descriptive observations only. Reaching London does not restore a strictly controlled A/C comparison. The actual arrival observations for A and C are retained separately. Now we return to A: the whole army taking the direct route.

Over that period, gold fell from about 637.55 to 621.48. The net decrease was 16.06. That is the net balance change after all income and expenses. It is not a march-cost ledger or a verified embarkation payment. Now consider C's replay using a different route. From the shared start to its arrival observation, gold decreased by about 15.82 net. That figure is also only a net change. During embarkation, we observed a net decrease of 17 gold. In another window, it increased by about 0.25 net. Neither cause is established by an itemized payment ledger. A and C now each have an actual arrival observation. B stopped after failing the fixed conditions. C also retains its sampling deviations. This run cannot establish a winner in a strictly controlled three-plan comparison.

We observed full supply, actual reinforcement, and soldier decreases in separate windows. We also observed supply and roster changes during same-day splits and merges. Later rest periods produced actual increases in supply and soldier counts. The whole-army direct route and the alternate route each retain an actual arrival observation. The split-army plan stopped after its fixed conditions changed. The alternate-route replay retains sampling deviations. So there is no strictly controlled three-plan verdict. Actual starvation and itemized payments still need their own evidence. You can read your own army in this order. Give every new conclusion its own date, identity and observed result.
